phonemes.desc: Fully voiced dental stop [d] releasing directly into a trilled [r]; Old Norse initial d is unaspirated, and the cluster is voiced throughout.
The falling diphthong [ɑu] — open back [ɑ] gliding to [u], the sound Old Norse wrote au, cousin to the 'ow' of English 'cow'.
Voiceless bilabial [p], alveolar nasal [n], short close [i], and the final trilled [r] of the agent suffix -nir, the same ending as in Mjǫllnir.

pronunciation.approximation: 'DROYP-nir' — two syllables, stress on the first; 'droyp' rhyming with 'cowp', the au a single gliding vowel, the r's trilled.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Draupnir, Óðinn's ring, from the verb drjúpa 'to drip' with the agent suffix -nir: 'the dripper'. Völuspá's catalogue of dwarfs also knows a dwarf Draupnir.

kin.label: Younger Futhark
kin.form: ᛏᚱᛅᚢᛒᚾᛁᛦ (t-r-au-b-n-i-R) — the sixteen-rune Viking-Age rendering, with ᛏ writing the voiced d, ᛒ writing p, and ᛦ the final nominative -r.

kin.label: Modern Icelandic
kin.form: Draupnir — still current as a name for ships, companies, and horses, the dripper unbroken in the language that kept the myths.

pronunciation.note: Draupnir is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter — so the ASCII alphabet loses nothing in copying it. The richest treasure in Ásgarðr wears one of its plainest names; only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input.

domains.title: Odin's Ring, Wealth
domains.subtitle: The Dripper of the Ninth Night
domains.lead: Draupnir is the golden arm-ring of Óðinn, forged by the dwarf Sindri while his brother Brokkr worked the bellows — the one treasure in the northern corpus that increases by its own nature. Every ninth night eight new rings of equal weight drip from it, so that the Allfather's wealth is not a hoard but a fountain. Óðinn laid it on Baldr's pyre as his last gift to his son, and Baldr sent it back from Hel with Hermóðr: the ring that crosses the boundary of death in both directions.

cards.name: Sindri's Forge
cards.desc: The dwarf-smith's hearth where gold went in and the ring came out — Brokkr at the bellows, forbidden to stop, and a fly on his hand.

cards.name: The Eight Rings
cards.desc: Every ninth night, eight rings of equal weight drip from the one — wealth that multiplies in the dark, without labour and without theft.

cards.name: Baldr's Pyre
cards.desc: The ring Óðinn laid on Hringhorni's fire beside his dead son — the father's parting gift, sent into the smoke with the fairest of the Æsir.

cards.name: Hermóðr's Return
cards.desc: The token Baldr sent back from Hel's hall with the nine-night rider — proof, in gold, that the errand reached the dead god's hand.

symbols.name: The gold ring itself
symbols.meaning: Wealth that breeds wealth — the one treasure in the corpus whose nature is increase, not keeping

symbols.name: The ninth night
symbols.meaning: The interval of multiplication — eight rings of equal weight for every nine nights the ring is kept

symbols.name: Brokkr's bellows
symbols.meaning: The unbroken breath of the forge — the wager turned on a blast no fly could interrupt twice

symbols.name: The fly (Loki)
symbols.meaning: The sting that cost the hammer its handle but could not touch the ring — malice spent against patience

symbols.name: The pyre-token
symbols.meaning: The gift that goes down with the dead and returns with the messenger — love's keepsake across Hel's gate

mythology.lead: Draupnir's dossier divides cleanly in two: Skáldskaparmál tells its making, in the wager that also produced Gullinbursti and Mjǫllnir, and the Baldr cycle tells its journey — into the fire with the dead god and back out of Hel with the living one's token. Between those poles the Poetic Edda catches it twice: offered and refused in Skírnismál, and catalogued as a dwarf's own name in Völuspá.

myths.title: The Wager of Loki's Head
myths.text:
It begins with a crime of Loki's: he cut off all the hair of Sif, Þórr's wife, for mischief. Þórr caught him and would have broken every bone in him, but Loki swore to get the black-elves to make Sif hair of gold that would grow like other hair. He went to the dwarfs called the sons of Ivaldi, and they made the golden hair, and Skíðblaðnir, the best of ships, for Freyr, and the spear Gungnir for Óðinn. Then Loki boasted, and his boasting made the bet: he wagered his own head with the dwarf Brokkr that Brokkr's brother Sindri could not make three treasures as good as these.

Snorri frames the whole episode as an explanation of how the gods got their treasures — the myth exists in the Edda to account for the properties of the great objects, and Draupnir's property is the strangest of them: it does not merely exist; it multiplies.

myths.title: Three Treasures from the Bellows
myths.text:
Sindri laid a pig's skin in the forge and told Brokkr to blow, and never to stop until he himself drew the work out. When the smith had gone from the forge, a fly settled on Brokkr's hand and stung him — but he blew on. Out came the boar with bristles of gold, Gullinbursti. Next Sindri laid gold in the forge and gave the same command; the fly settled on Brokkr's neck and stung twice as hard — but he blew on. Out came the ring Draupnir. Last came iron, and the fly settled between Brokkr's eyes and stung the eyelid until blood ran down and blinded him; he swept the fly away with his hand, and for that one moment the bellows failed — and so the hammer Mjǫllnir came out with its handle too short. The fly was Loki, spending himself against the bellows.

The brothers carried the three treasures to Ásgarðr to be judged against Loki's three. Óðinn received the spear Gungnir and the ring Draupnir, and Snorri gives the ring's nature in a single sentence the whole tradition repeats: every ninth night, eight rings of equal weight drip from it. Freyr took the ship and the boar; Þórr took the hammer. The Æsir judged Mjǫllnir the best of all, because it was the surest defence against the rime-giants — but Loki kept his head on a point of law: Brokkr might have the head, but not one hair of the neck. So the dwarf sewed Loki's lips shut instead, and the wager closed with the gods six treasures richer.

myths.title: The Ring Refused
myths.text:
The Poetic Edda catches the ring in motion, being offered as a bride-price. When Freyr's servant Skírnir rides to Jötunheimr to woo the giant's daughter Gerðr for his lovesick master, he carries gifts, and the second of them is the ring: 'the ring that was burned with Óðinn's young son; eight of equal weight drip from it every ninth night.' The poem does not name it — it does not need to; no other ring in the corpus matches the description, and the tradition from the prose commentators onward has read it as Draupnir.

Gerðr refuses it: she wants no gold, she says, for she lacks none in her father Gymir's halls, and will not share wealth with Freyr's messenger. The episode is a quiet marvel of the corpus: the self-breeding ring of the Allfather, the one gift that cannot be outbid, laid before a giantess who counts it worthless. Only Skírnir's curse, carved in runes and threats, moves her where Óðinn's treasure could not — the poem's own verdict that gold, even multiplying gold, buys nothing that matters.

myths.title: The Ring on the Pyre
myths.text:
When Baldr lay dead of the mistletoe and the Æsir built his pyre on Hringhorni, the greatest of ships, the funeral gathered the whole wealth of the gods' grief. Nanna died of sorrow at the sight of him and was laid beside her husband; Þórr hallowed the pyre with Mjǫllnir; and Óðinn did the thing this temple exists to record: he laid the ring Draupnir on the fire with his son. No word of his is preserved with the gift. The dripper, the fountain of the Allfather's gold, went into the smoke as a father's last giving to the child he could not keep.

The corpus keeps the gesture where it belongs — among the funeral's few named acts, beside the hallowing hammer and the burst heart. A ring that makes eight more of itself every ninth night is the least losable treasure in the world, and Óðinn loses it deliberately, which is exactly what makes it a gift.

myths.title: Back from Hel, and the Dwarf's Name
myths.text:
The story does not let the ring rest in the fire. Hermóðr the Bold rode nine nights down the dark road, leapt Helgrindr on Sleipnir, and found Baldr seated in the high seat of Hel's hall. When Hel set her famous condition — that all things in the world must weep Baldr out — Baldr sent tokens home with the rider, and first among them was Draupnir, returned to Óðinn as a keepsake. The ransom failed at Þökk's one refusal, and Baldr stayed with the dead; but the ring came back across the boundary that nothing else crosses, carrying the dead god's love to the living father. It is the only object in the corpus to make that journey in both directions.

Völuspá preserves the name's older, stranger root: in the dvergatal, the great catalogue of dwarfs, a dwarf named Draupnir stands in the list beside Dólgþrasir and his kin. The treasure-name and the dwarf-name are the same word — 'the dripper' — and scholars have long noted how naturally the corpus names its wonders after its smiths. The ring that drips gold wears a name the dwarf-lists already owned, as if the Edda kept, fossilized in its oldest poem, the memory that such things come from under the earth.

lore.syncretism: Draupnir needs no borrowed god to explain it — it is an object, and its company is other objects. The corpus itself sets the sharpest contrast: [[andvari|Andvari]]'s ring Andvaranaut, extorted at the waterfall and cursed, kills every hand that holds it, while Draupnir, freely made for the gods on a wager's terms, breeds gold for its keeper — the taken ring destroys, the given ring multiplies. The wider Germanic context is the ring-giving culture the poetry everywhere assumes: Beowulf's lord is the *beaga brytta*, the 'ring-giver', and arm-rings were the very currency of loyalty between lord and man; a self-breeding ring is that economy's dream made metal. Folklorists file Draupnir among the self-multiplying magic treasures of the international motif-index, beside inexhaustible purses and cornucopias; its nearest mythic cousins are things, not gods. Within the corpus its makers [[brokkr|Brokkr]] and [[sindri|Sindri]] and its fellow-wonders — Gullinbursti, and [[thor|Þórr]]'s hammer [[mjolnir|Mjǫllnir]] from the same forging — are its true kin.
lore.culturalLegacy: Draupnir's afterlife is the afterlife of an idea: the treasure that makes treasure. Nineteenth-century retellings fixed the forging-wager as a set-piece of the Norse revival — the Kearys' The Heroes of Asgard (1857) carries Brokkr and Sindri at the bellows, and every handbook since repeats the ninth-night dripping. In modern popular culture the name has become a byword for self-replicating wonders: God of War Ragnarök (2022) gives Brok and Sindri a Draupnir of its own — a spear, forged from the ring's multiplying magic, that reproduces itself in the wielder's hand — the most widely seen adaptation of the dwarf-brothers and their craft in any medium. Fantasy games and fiction reach for the name whenever gear must breed gear. In Iceland the word never needed reviving: Draupnir remains a living name there for ships, firms, and horses, the dripper doing ordinary work in the language that wrote the Eddas. And every time a modern storyteller needs wealth that grows honestly — by time, by patience, by nature rather than by taking — the shape they reach for is Óðinn's ring, whether they name it or not.
lore.extendedMeditation: The North was not sentimental about gold. Its greatest hoard is cursed at birth, its dragons die on their beds of metal, and its poets ken gold as the fire of the flood where the Niflungar sank it. Against all of that stands one exception, and it is the highest treasure of the highest god: a ring whose only property is that it increases. Draupnir does not shine, speak, strike, or protect. It drips — on a schedule, in the dark, eight for one every ninth night, wealth arriving the way wealth actually arrives for those who keep it lawfully: slowly, cyclically, and by nature rather than by conquest. The myth then does the two most instructive things a myth can do with such an object. It gives it away: Óðinn lays the one inexhaustible treasure in the world on his son's pyre, because no fountain of gold outweighs one act of love. And it sends it back: the dead return the gift to the living, because some bonds outlast the boundary. Between those two gestures the ring becomes something stranger than a treasure — a measure of what treasure is for. The cursed ring of the dwarf [[andvari|Andvari]] passes from hand to hand and each owner dies; the dripper passes from father to son and back to father, and the only thing that multiplies is the meaning. Gold that is kept breeds gold. Gold that is given breeds everything else.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Draupnir — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛏᚱᛅᚢᛒᚾᛁᛦ (t-r-au-b-n-i-R, the ᛏ-rune writing d, ᛒ writing p, and ᛦ the final nominative -r). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way: draupnir.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Draupnir is a literary object: no inscription names it, and no find can be identified with it — but the ring it describes belonged to one of the best-attested object-classes in the northern record. Gold and silver arm-rings are the standard currency of Viking-Age hoards: the great Gotlandic deposits, crowned by the Spillings hoard of 1999 (the largest Viking silver hoard yet found), are full of ring-money cut and weighed as bullion, the archaeological reality behind the poetry's ring-giver. The ring's social weight is documented from both sides of the conversion: Eyrbyggja saga (ch. 4) describes a twenty-ounce ring lying on the altar of the hof at Þórsnes, on which all oaths were sworn, and the Forsa ring of Hälsingland — an iron oath-ring bearing a runic law inscription, the oldest legal text in Scandinavia — survives as the practice's one famous material witness. Earlier still, the ring-swords of the Vendel-period elite, with a ring mounted on the pommel as the sign of the oath between lord and man (attested at Valsgärde and famously at Sutton Hoo), show the ring as the badge of the gift-bond itself. The manuscript witnesses are the usual two codices: Skáldskaparmál and Gylfaginning in the Codex Regius of the Prose Edda (GKS 2367 4to, c. 1300–1350), Skírnismál and Völuspá in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270).
